Faster for the supplied synthetic workload. Variant B reduced median end-to-end export time by 21.1%, from 152.072 ms to 119.945 ms, across nine alternating runs per side. This is a 1.268x throughput ratio. The job is CPU-bound on one worker, with JSON encoding its largest profiled component.

| Timed path | A median and range, ms | B median and range, ms | Runs per side |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| export, including record construction and UTF-8 conversion | 152.072, 146.123 to 161.819 | 119.945, 115.440 to 134.269 | 9 |
| encode_rows, serialization only | 115.503, 110.485 to 133.846 | 77.589, 71.662 to 92.604 | 9 |

The end-to-end ranges do not overlap. The 32.127 ms median gap exceeds each side's full range width, so no close-call rank-sum test was needed. This is a local repeated measurement, not a cross-machine estimate.

The measurement used the requested 20,000 records, one worker, Python 3.14.4, UTF-8, sorted keys, compact separators and in-memory output. Both sides use identical explicit encoder options and the same deterministic data. No debug/release distinction, configurable batching, storage transaction or pool setting exists in the supplied fixture. Each path had one excluded warmup per side, then A/B alternation for all nine pairs. GC stayed at its Python default. The serialization-only path reused an already-built record list. End-to-end export rebuilt the records inside every timed call, matching the application entrypoint. The before-run claim, environment, process snapshot and hashes are in [metadata.json](metadata.json).

`measure.py` times synchronous calls with `perf_counter_ns` and records process CPU time alongside them. It creates the complete string or byte result inside the timed interval. After the interval, it consumes that result for hashing, exact byte comparison and parsing. Correctness checking and file output are excluded from timing. The separate profile calls are excluded from reported timings. A process snapshot and load averages show a lightly loaded four-core host, with load 0.24 / 0.38 / 0.39 before and 0.36 / 0.40 / 0.40 after. Other processes were not changed.

The CPU evidence supports a one-core encoding limiter. Median process CPU time is 151.916 ms for A and 119.612 ms for B, close to elapsed time. Separate cProfile runs show `exporter.py:14 encode_rows` consuming 0.202 of 0.270 profile seconds in A and 0.136 of 0.218 in B. `encoder.py:207 iterencode` has the largest internal cost in A, 0.083 seconds, and ties record construction as the largest component in B, 0.075 seconds each. `exporter.py:16` calls `json.dumps` 20,000 times; B's `exporter.py:19` calls an existing encoder directly. Encoder construction falls from 20,000 calls to one. Full cumulative and internal-time tables are in [profile-A.txt](profile-A.txt) and [profile-B.txt](profile-B.txt), with binary `.pstats` files retained.

The measured difference is for the complete B code path. It includes bypassing the `json.dumps` wrapper and its repeated keyword dispatch, as well as reusing the encoder. It does not isolate encoder construction alone. In the A profile, encoder construction accounts for only about 0.007 of 0.270 seconds. Removing only that component would allow roughly 1.027x speedup in that instrumented run, so constructor cost alone would not explain a 1.268x end-to-end timing ratio. Profile overhead changes absolute costs and these fractions are diagnostic, not production timings.

The output is 2,571,113 bytes per call, giving about 16.91 MB/s for A and 21.44 MB/s for B. There is no disk or network transfer in the timed path, so disk/network bandwidth limits do not apply. Process CPU cost is about 7.60 microseconds per record for A and 5.98 for B. The corresponding record rates consume about one core, consistent with a single-worker CPU job and below the four available cores. No memory bandwidth ceiling was measured.

The serialization microbenchmark is approximately 76.0% of the baseline export median. Its 37.914 ms median improvement is of the same order as the 32.127 ms end-to-end improvement; independent timings and allocation/warmth differences mean they are not an exact additive decomposition. Eliminating the entire measured baseline serialization share would permit at most about 4.16x throughput. The observed 1.268x ratio is below this bound. The remaining record creation, hashing and UTF-8 conversion explain why serialization improvement is diluted end to end.

All 42 checked calls passed, covering 36 measured calls, four warmups and two profile calls. Each result has 20,000 actual newline separators, zero literal backslash-n separators, 20,000 independently expected rows, matching UTF-8 content and an identical byte hash. Parsing verifies every ID, name, active flag and SHA-256 fingerprint; exact serialization verifies sorted keys and compact separators. a=s['export']['A'];b=s['export']['B']; ma=s['encode_rows']['A']; mb=s['encode_rows']['B']
report=f'''Faster for the supplied synthetic workload. Variant B reduced median end-to-end export time by {s['export']['elapsed_reduction_pct']:.1f}%, from {a['median_ms']:.3f} ms to {b['median_ms']:.3f} ms, across nine alternating runs per side. This is a {s['export']['throughput_speedup']:.3f}x throughput ratio. The job is CPU-bound on one worker, with JSON encoding its largest profiled component.

| Timed path | A median and range, ms | B median and range, ms | Runs per side |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| export, including record construction and UTF-8 conversion | {a['median_ms']:.3f}, {a['min_ms']:.3f} to {a['max_ms']:.3f} | {b['median_ms']:.3f}, {b['min_ms']:.3f} to {b['max_ms']:.3f} | 9 |
| encode_rows, serialization only | {ma['median_ms']:.3f}, {ma['min_ms']:.3f} to {ma['max_ms']:.3f} | {mb['median_ms']:.3f}, {mb['min_ms']:.3f} to {mb['max_ms']:.3f} | 9 |

The end-to-end ranges do not overlap. The 32.127 ms median gap exceeds each side's full range width, so no close-call rank-sum test was needed. This is a local repeated measurement, not a cross-machine estimate.

The measurement used the requested 20,000 records, one worker, Python 3.14.4, UTF-8, sorted keys, compact separators and in-memory output. Both sides use identical explicit encoder options and the same deterministic data. No debug/release distinction, configurable batching, storage transaction or pool setting exists in the supplied fixture. Each path had one excluded warmup per side, then A/B alternation for all nine pairs. GC stayed at its Python default. The serialization-only path reused an already-built record list. End-to-end export rebuilt the records inside every timed call, matching the application entrypoint. The before-run claim, environment, process snapshot and hashes are in [metadata.json](metadata.json).

`measure.py` times synchronous calls with `perf_counter_ns` and records process CPU time alongside them. It creates the complete string or byte result inside the timed interval. After the interval, it consumes that result for hashing, exact byte comparison and parsing. Correctness checking and file output are excluded from timing. The separate profile calls are excluded from reported timings. A process snapshot and load averages show a lightly loaded four-core host, with load 0.24 / 0.38 / 0.39 before and 0.36 / 0.40 / 0.40 after. Other processes were not changed.

The CPU evidence supports a one-core encoding limiter. Median process CPU time is {a['median_cpu_ms']:.3f} ms for A and {b['median_cpu_ms']:.3f} ms for B, close to elapsed time. Separate cProfile runs show `exporter.py:14 encode_rows` consuming 0.202 of 0.270 profile seconds in A and 0.136 of 0.218 in B. `encoder.py:207 iterencode` has the largest internal cost in A, 0.083 seconds, and ties record construction as the largest component in B, 0.075 seconds each. `exporter.py:16` calls `json.dumps` 20,000 times; B's `exporter.py:19` calls an existing encoder directly. Encoder construction falls from 20,000 calls to one. Full cumulative and internal-time tables are in [profile-A.txt](profile-A.txt) and [profile-B.txt](profile-B.txt), with binary `.pstats` files retained.

The measured difference is for the complete B code path. It includes bypassing the `json.dumps` wrapper and its repeated keyword dispatch, as well as reusing the encoder. It does not isolate encoder construction alone. In the A profile, encoder construction accounts for only about 0.007 of 0.270 seconds. Removing only that component would allow roughly 1.027x speedup in that instrumented run, so constructor cost alone would not explain a 1.268x end-to-end timing ratio. Profile overhead changes absolute costs and these fractions are diagnostic, not production timings.

The output is {check['bytes']:,} bytes per call, giving about {check['bytes']/a['median_ms']/1000:.2f} MB/s for A and {check['bytes']/b['median_ms']/1000:.2f} MB/s for B. There is no disk or network transfer in the timed path, so disk/network bandwidth limits do not apply. Process CPU cost is about {a['median_cpu_ms']*1000/20000:.2f} microseconds per record for A and {b['median_cpu_ms']*1000/20000:.2f} for B. The corresponding record rates consume about one core, consistent with a single-worker CPU job and below the four available cores. No memory bandwidth ceiling was measured.

The serialization microbenchmark is approximately {100*ma['median_ms']/a['median_ms']:.1f}% of the baseline export median. Its 37.914 ms median improvement is of the same order as the 32.127 ms end-to-end improvement; independent timings and allocation/warmth differences mean they are not an exact additive decomposition. Eliminating the entire measured baseline serialization share would permit at most about {1/(1-ma['median_ms']/a['median_ms']):.2f}x throughput. The observed 1.268x ratio is below this bound. The remaining record creation, hashing and UTF-8 conversion explain why serialization improvement is diluted end to end.

All 42 checked calls passed, covering 36 measured calls, four warmups and two profile calls. Each result has 20,000 actual newline separators, zero literal backslash-n separators, 20,000 independently expected rows, matching UTF-8 content and an identical byte hash. Parsing verifies every ID, name, active flag and SHA-256 fingerprint; exact serialization verifies sorted keys and compact separators. There were zero fixture exceptions, zero content failures and zero NDJSON failures in the completed run. The shared output SHA-256 is `{check['sha256']}`. SHA-256 provenance:

| Input | SHA-256 |
| --- | --- |
'''
for path,h in m['hashes'].items():
